## Findings by module

### investing-6

- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Mackay (1841) on the Dutch tulip mania of 1634-1637: the turning point in his telling is when the rich no longer bought tulips to keep in their gardens but to sell again at a hundred per cent profit, exactly Graham's line between investment and speculation; at first everyone gained, people of every rank turned property into cash to buy bulbs, everyone imagined the passion would last for ever, then the prudent saw that somebody must lose, prices fell and never rose again, and bulbs could not be sold even at a quarter of their cost. Use as the historical case inside the investment-or-speculation lesson.
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): Mackay: after the tulip collapse, buyers refused contracts struck at 4,000 florins when the price had fallen to 300 or 400; the courts refused to enforce what they called gambling debts, so holders bore their ruin and those who had sold kept their profits, and Dutch commerce took years to recover. Caution for the lesson: Mackay wrote two centuries later and his account is a popular retelling, so quote his pattern, not his prices, as fact (our caution).
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Mackay on 1720, the UK case: among the 'bubble' companies one unknown promoter advertised 'a company for carrying on an undertaking of great advantage, but nobody to know what it is', asking a 2 deposit per 100 share and promising 100 a year per share, with details 'in a month'; a thousand shares were taken in five hours and he left for the Continent with 2,000, never heard of again. A 300-year-old version of today's scam warning signs (vague business, huge promised return, pressure to pay a deposit now). Strong case for the scams lesson.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Mackay: Robert Walpole warned Parliament that the South Sea scheme would lure the unwary to part with the earnings of their labour for imaginary wealth, raising the stock artificially by keeping up a general infatuation and promising dividends from funds that could never be adequate; he was ignored and the benches emptied when he spoke. Directors spread rumours of Spanish trade concessions to lift the price; many buyers did not believe in the schemes at all but expected to sell at a premium to the really credulous. Shows rumour-driven promotion and buying to pass on to someone more gullible.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Mackay: South Sea stock rose to 1,000 per cent by early August 1720 and fell to 135 by the end of September; in the space of eight months it rose and fell. It became known that the chairman, Sir John Blunt, and other insiders had sold out while still promoting; a false rumour of Bank of England support lifted the price for an afternoon. The poet John Gay was urged by friends to sell enough to secure a hundred a year for life, refused while dreaming of splendour, and lost profit and principal. Use the Gay story beside Fisher's 1929 remark: insiders sell, and the refusal to take a secure gain is the behavioural trap.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Mackay: during the bubble, people were no longer satisfied with the slow but sure profits of cautious industry; the hope of boundless wealth tomorrow made them heedless today. The run spread to goldsmiths who had lent on South Sea stock, some of whom absconded. A plain statement of why slow, steady investing loses its appeal in a boom.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Mackay: Parliament's Committee of Secrecy found the South Sea books falsified (fictitious entries, blanks, torn-out leaves), and fictitious stock given as bribes to ministers to pass the bill; the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Aislabie, was expelled and sent to the Tower. The scheme had Act-of-Parliament backing and ministerial champions. Lesson for the scams module: official backing, famous names and a respectable front are not protection; check who profits from your purchase.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Mackay's conclusion: in times of prosperity the success of one project produces others of the same kind, and popular imitation drags a community too anxious for profit into an abyss (the 1825 panic repeated the 1720 pattern); the lesson is how dangerous it is to hope for enormous profits from inadequate causes. Herd behaviour and copy-cat schemes as a recurring cycle, not a one-off.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Mackay on John Law (1716-1720): Law's bank first did real good, its notes holding value while state paper traded at a 78.5 per cent discount; because the bank had done so much good, any promise Law made for the future was readily believed. Once the bank became royal, notes worth 1,000 million livres were printed against Law's own rule that issuing paper without funds deserved death. A genuine early success is what makes the later, unfounded promises credible: past results are not evidence for new promises.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Mackay on 1719 Paris: two philosophers, La Motte and the Abbé Terrasson, congratulated each other on being free of the Mississippi mania and met days later at the share office, each going to buy; they agreed that no extravagance is beyond even a wise man. A memorable case for the behaviour lesson: knowing about bubbles does not make you immune, so write rules in advance (fear of missing out).
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Mackay: Law promised a yearly dividend of 200 livres on each 500-livre share, which on the depreciated state paper used to pay for it was about 120 per cent a year; 300,000 applications came for 50,000 new shares, then 300,000 more shares were created at 5,000 livres. Prices sometimes rose 10 or 20 per cent in hours, and servants and coachmen became suddenly rich. An extreme promised return plus stories of easy wealth among ordinary people are the classic signs of a mania.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Mackay: the shrewd dealers who guessed prices could not rise for ever quietly converted notes to coin in small amounts and sent it abroad, one smuggling nearly a million livres under hay and dung, while the public kept buying; a parade of 6,000 conscripted 'miners' for Louisiana briefly lifted the shares among the gullible. Insiders leave quietly and staged good news props up a failing scheme.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Mackay: John Law never doubted his scheme, invested all his gains in French land, sent nothing abroad, and left France almost a beggar, dying in debt in Venice in 1729. Sincere conviction by the cleverest person in the room is no protection: like Fisher in 1929, the expert who believes most has the most to lose. Pairs with the course's Fisher case.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Mackay: as the paper fell, many large holders refused to convert into safe 2.5 per cent city annuities and kept the falling paper in the hope of a favourable turn, until edicts made the notes worthless after November 1720. Holding a falling asset in the hope it will come back (loss aversion) as a recurring bubble behaviour. A period epigram compresses the arc: shares bought Monday, millions Tuesday, carriage Thursday, ball Friday, poorhouse Saturday.
- **extended** (ch-001.txt): Mackay's preface: sober nations have suddenly become desperate gamblers, risking almost everything on a piece of paper; men think in herds, go mad in herds, and recover their senses only slowly, one by one. The core statement of herd behaviour, usable (short quote under 15 words) in the biases lesson.
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Mackay 1720 timeline: South Sea stock went from 130 to about 300 when the Commons took up the scheme in February, near 400 during the bill, subscriptions sold at 300 and then 400 per cent; nearly a hundred bubble companies were floated, and the Crown proclaimed them public nuisances on 11 June 1720 and dissolved them on 12 July. (Mackay's figures; check against a modern history before quoting precisely.)
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Mackay's verdict: the public blamed only the directors, but nobody blamed the credulity and avarice of the people that made the multitude run into the net. A balanced reminder for the behaviour lesson that the buyer's own greed is part of every bubble.

### investing-1

- **extended** (ch-002.txt): Mackay on 1719-1720 France: as paper notes multiplied to keep pace with share prices, goods paid for in paper rose four-fold, bread and meat reached record prices, and wages rose in the same proportion, an illusory prosperity. By May 1720, 2,600 million livres of notes stood against coin worth under half that; the state banned holding more than 500 livres in coin, tried to halve the notes' value, and the bank stopped paying in coin on 27 May. A vivid historical case of money printed without backing turning into inflation and loss for those holding paper.
- **note** (ch-002.txt): Mackay: the French Regency's 1715 recoinage cut the metal in each coin by a fifth while keeping its face value, gaining the treasury 72 million livres and disordering commerce: an early example of currency debasement, a form of inflation that quietly transfers wealth from holders of money to the issuer.
